sources.news_title: Tennessee’s prisons chief is resigning after failed execution of Christa Pike - Boston News, Weather, Sports
sources.text:
The head of Tennessee’s prison system is resigning, Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday, the first major staff shake-up since Christa Pike’s stunning failed execution left her unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital.
Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, will step down this month, Lee said. Some of the governor’s fellow Republicans and other elected officials had been urging a change in leadership.
It was the second time since May that Tennessee has not been able to execute a prisoner who was seemingly moments away from death.
The governor also announced that former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton would lead a review of what happened in Pike’s death chamber. Stanton previously was named to conduct a review after Lee called off a different execution in 2022; he found in that case that Tennessee had not complied with its own lethal injection process.
Strada said in a statement that resigning was “in the best interest of Tennesseans” while Stanton’s review is conducted. The state failed to execute Pike despite administering two doses of a lethal drug, pentobarbital.
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.
Strada defends execution protocol
There was no immediate response from Pike’s lawyers for an update Saturday on her condition at a hospital. They had disclosed Friday that she was on a ventilator and unconscious in the hours following the execution attempt and that hospital staff were trying to clear the two doses of pentobarbital.
The shocking failure has left both sides of the death penalty debate demanding answers. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted any new executions. Strada said he believes the state “carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol.”
Pike’s legal team welcomed Strada’s departure but said “it does nothing to help Christa now.”
“What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person,” the four-lawyer team said. “We hope the governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system.”
Second failed execution since May
Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
Pike was extraordinarily cooperative with the execution team, even instructing them to “please try here, please try here” as they tried to insert lines, lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters Thursday.
In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm but couldn’t get a secondary IV line. The governor ordered officials to wait at least a year before trying to execute him again.
Strada took over the Correction Department in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections. In late 2024, he announced that Tennessee was changing its lethal injection protocol and would use only pentobarbital.
Four people have been executed in Tennessee since 2025, according to the Correction Department.
Some Arizona executions had snags
Court filings show that Strada’s job included overseeing executions in Arizona when they resumed in 2022 following an eight-year break.
Clarence Dixon was the first that year. The medical team had trouble finding a vein to administer the lethal drugs and finally made an incision in his groin area. The process took about 25 minutes.
That same year in Arizona, medical staff preparing Frank Atwood for execution initially could not locate a vein in his right arm but inserted the IV in his right hand — at Atwood’s suggestion, said Henry Brean, an Arizona Daily Star reporter who was a witness.
Strada announced Murray Hooper’s execution by lethal injection, the third in 2022. There was an unsuccessful attempt to insert an IV line in his right arm. The IV in Hooper’s leg was inserted into his femoral artery.
“When Governor Lee hired Strada to fix execution problems in Tennessee, his problematic history of executions in Arizona was well known,” said Kit Thomas, an attorney who has represented people on Tennessee’s death row.

sources.news_title: Top Official Resigns After Execution Disaster
sources.text:
Top Official Resigns After Execution Disaster
Tennessee’s corrections commissioner resigned after a lethal injection of Christa Pike failed, leaving her alive and on a ventilator, and the state halted its remaining executions for the year.
Commissioner Frank Strada stepped down after the Wednesday night attempt. Gov. Bill Lee announced the resignation on October 3 and said an independent review would examine what went wrong. Strada had led the department since January 2023 and, in late 2024, said Tennessee would use only pentobarbital.
Pike, 50, received two doses. Staff used at least seven needles trying to find a vein. A Friday court filing from her lawyers said she cried, whimpered and breathed loudly. She was taken to a hospital, intubated and placed on a ventilator. The filing said staff mis-set the IV lines and missed that a vein had burst, so at least some of the drug entered her body.
Pike was convicted of the January 12, 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. At 18, Pike lured Slemmer into woods near the University of Tennessee’s agricultural campus. She and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, tortured Slemmer for about 30 minutes while 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson kept watch. Pike told investigators she believed Slemmer was interested in Shipp.
She was sentenced to death and became one of the youngest women sent to death row. An execution would have been the first of a woman in Tennessee since 1819. Shipp, 17 at the time, received life with parole and has not been released. Peterson pleaded guilty as an accessory, testified, and served 460 days.
Strada said stepping aside was “in the best interest of Tennesseans” and that the review was “entirely appropriate and necessary.” Lee said Strada had served with integrity and praised his “willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment.”
Pike’s lawyers said the failure “reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person” and hoped the review would “expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system.”
Lee asked the attorney general’s office to hire former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton for the review. Stanton led a 2022 review of the state’s lethal-injection protocol that forced a rewrite before executions resumed. The new review will ask whether protocol was followed and what should change. Lee postponed the remaining execution on this year’s calendar until that work is done.

sources.news_title: Tennessee Prison Chief Who Oversaw Botched Execution Of Christa Pike Resigns
sources.text:
The prison chief in the southern US state of Tennessee has resigned, the governor said Saturday, after an unprecedented botched execution left a convicted murderer on a ventilator in critical condition.
Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada will leave his post this month, Governor Bill Lee said in a statement.
Christa Pike, 50, on Wednesday survived two lethal injections of pentobarbital, a drug that suppresses nervous system activity.
Media witnesses listened to her snoring for about an hour after being administered the deadly doses, and said she was alive as they were ushered out of the execution chamber viewing area at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.
Pike was taken to a hospital where she was “critically ill,” unconscious and on a ventilator as medical staff worked to clear the pentobarbital from her system, her lawyers said in a court filing Friday.
Lee said he thanked Strada for “his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment.”
In the same statement, Strada said: “I continue to believe the Department (of Correction) carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol.”
Lee, who previously denied Pike clemency, has halted further executions through the rest of the year pending a “comprehensive, third-party review.”
– Caustic –
Pike’s legal team had previously objected to the execution’s IV protocol, saying it would have caused needless suffering due to her small veins and a blood condition.
Lawyer Randy Spivey has said he saw seven needles used in just Pike’s left arm as execution staff tried to start an IV line, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt.”
Medical experts had warned of needles becoming dislodged or piercing through the vein, causing lethal drugs to flow into Pike’s arm instead of the bloodstream, lawyer Stephen Ferrell has said.
The court filing described pentobarbital as a caustic substance that burns skin, tissue and veins. Upon arrival at the hospital, both of Pike’s arms were “swollen, burned, and blistered,” it said.
Media witnesses said Pike told execution staff after receiving the lethal injection that her arm felt like it would “burst open.”
The Death Penalty Information Center, which publishes data and analysis on capital punishment in the United States, said Pike was the first inmate ever to survive “after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs.”
Her case had sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals, as she was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp.
The 1995 killing gained national attention after Slemmer’s body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.
Pike’s lawyers had argued for clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of Slemmer’s killing. They also cited her history of childhood sexual assault and post-traumatic stress disorder.
The case had already attracted attention in the lead-up to the execution date as Pike would have been the first woman put to death by the state of Tennessee in more than 200 years.
In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

sources.news_title: US prison chief Frank Strada who oversaw botched Christa Pike execution resigns
sources.text:
Christa Pike, 50, survived two lethal injections of pentobarbital on Wednesday
Washington, United States: The prison chief in the southern US state of Tennessee has resigned, the governor said Saturday, after an unprecedented botched execution left a convicted murderer on a ventilator in critical condition.
Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada will leave his post this month, Governor Bill Lee said in a statement.
Get updated faster and for FREE: Download the Gulf News app now - simply click here.
Christa Pike, 50, on Wednesday survived two lethal injections of pentobarbital, a drug that suppresses nervous system activity.
Media witnesses listened to her snoring for about an hour after being administered the deadly doses, and said she was alive as they were ushered out of the execution chamber viewing area at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.
Pike was taken to a hospital where she was "critically ill," unconscious and on a ventilator as medical staff worked to clear the pentobarbital from her system, her lawyers said in a court filing Friday.
Lee said he thanked Strada for "his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment."
In the same statement, Strada said: "I continue to believe the Department (of Correction) carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol."
Lee, who previously denied Pike clemency, has halted further executions through the rest of the year pending a "comprehensive, third-party review."
Pike's legal team had previously objected to the execution's IV protocol, saying it would have caused needless suffering due to her small veins and a blood condition.
Lawyer Randy Spivey has said he saw seven needles used in just Pike's left arm as execution staff tried to start an IV line, "one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt."
Medical experts had warned of needles becoming dislodged or piercing through the vein, causing lethal drugs to flow into Pike's arm instead of the bloodstream, lawyer Stephen Ferrell has said.
The court filing described pentobarbital as a caustic substance that burns skin, tissue and veins. Upon arrival at the hospital, both of Pike's arms were "swollen, burned, and blistered," it said.
Media witnesses said Pike told execution staff after receiving the lethal injection that her arm felt like it would "burst open."
The Death Penalty Information Center, which publishes data and analysis on capital punishment in the United States, said Pike was the first inmate ever to survive "after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs."
Her case had sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals, as she was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp.
The 1995 killing gained national attention after Slemmer's body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.
Pike's lawyers had argued for clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of Slemmer's killing. They also cited her history of childhood sexual assault and post-traumatic stress disorder.
The case had already attracted attention in the lead-up to the execution date as Pike would have been the first woman put to death by the state of Tennessee in more than 200 years.
In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

sources.news_title: Prison boss resigns over bungled execution of Pike
sources.text:
The prison commissioner in the southern US state of Tennessee has resigned over the botched execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike, Governor Bill Lee said on Saturday.
Lee said in a statement that commissioner Frank Strada would leave his post this month.
Pike's lawyers say she is in critical condition, unconscious and on a ventilator in a hospital, after her execution by lethal injection went wrong on Wednesday.
Pike, 50, survived two injections of the normally lethal substance pentobarbital as punishment for the murder of Colleen Slemmer in 1995.
It was the second failed execution in Tennessee this year. 
The state halted an execution in May after medical staff failed to tap a vein in the prisoner's arm.
Lee said he thanked Strada for "his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment."
In the same statement, Strada said, "I continue to believe the Department (of Correction) carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol."
Lee, who previously denied Pike clemency, has halted further executions through the rest of the year while a review is conducted.
Had the drugs killed Pike, she would have been the first woman executed by the state in more than two centuries.
In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. (AFP)

Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday that the head of Tennessee's prison system is resigning over the botched execution of murder accused Christa Pike.
This comes as the first major staff shake-up since Pike's stunning failed execution left her unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital.
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.
After a dramatic day of legal wrangling, prison officials in Tennessee on Wednesday injected two deadly doses of the highly toxic drug pentobarbital into Pike for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer.
But witnesses said that the 50-year-old Pike remained awake longer than expected and was later heard "loudly snoring" before an ambulance rushed her to a nearby hospital.
Pike's lawyers say she is in critical condition, unconscious and on a ventilator in a hospital, after her execution by lethal injection went wrong on Wednesday, news agency AFP reported.
It was the second failed execution in Tennessee this year. The state halted an execution in May after medical staff failed to tap a vein in the prisoner's arm.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has halted attempts to carry out the death penalty for the rest of 2026.
Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, will step down this month, Lee said. The governor said he thanked Strada for "his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment."
Meanwhile, Strada reportedly said, "I continue to believe the Department [of Correction] carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol."
Strada said in a statement that resigning was “in the best interest of Tennesseans” while former US Attorney Ed Stanton's review is conducted. The state failed to execute Pike despite administering two doses of a lethal drug, pentobarbital.
The governor announced that Stanton would lead a review of what happened in Pike's death chamber.
Stanton previously was named to conduct a review after Lee called off a different execution in 2022; he found in that case that Tennessee had not complied with its own lethal injection process.
An interim commissioner will be announced later, the governor's office said.
"Commissioner Strada has served with integrity, and I appreciate his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment,” Lee said in a statement.
There was no immediate response from Pike's lawyers for an update Saturday on her condition at a hospital. They had disclosed Friday that she was on a ventilator and unconscious in the hours following the execution attempt and that hospital staff were trying to clear the two doses of pentobarbital.
The shocking failure has left both sides of the death penalty debate demanding answers. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted any new executions. Strada said he believes the state “carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol.”
Pike's legal team welcomed Strada's departure but said “it does nothing to help Christa now.”
“What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person,” the four-lawyer team said. “We hope the governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system.”
Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
Pike was extraordinarily cooperative with the execution team, even instructing them to “please try here, please try here” as they tried to insert lines, lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters Thursday.
In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm but couldn’t get a secondary IV line. The governor ordered officials to wait at least a year before trying to execute him again.
Strada took over the Correction Department in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections. In late 2024, he announced that Tennessee was changing its lethal injection protocol and would use only pentobarbital.
Four people have been executed in Tennessee since 2025, according to the Correction Department.
Court filings show that Strada's job included overseeing executions in Arizona when they resumed in 2022 following an eight-year break.
Clarence Dixon was the first that year. The medical team had trouble finding a vein to administer the lethal drugs and finally made an incision in his groin area. The process took about 25 minutes.
That same year in Arizona, medical staff preparing Frank Atwood for execution initially could not locate a vein in his right arm but inserted the IV in his right hand — at Atwood’s suggestion, said Henry Brean, an Arizona Daily Star reporter who was a witness.
Strada announced Murray Hooper's execution by lethal injection, the third in 2022. There was an unsuccessful attempt to insert an IV line in his right arm. The IV in Hooper's leg was inserted into his femoral artery.
“When Governor Lee hired Strada to fix execution problems in Tennessee, his problematic history of executions in Arizona was well known,” said Kit Thomas, an attorney who has represented people on Tennessee's death row.
Had the drugs killed Pike, she would have been the first woman executed by the state in more than two centuries.
In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

sources.text:
TENNESSEE - The head of prisons in the US state of Tennessee is resigning after the failed execution of death row inmate Christa Pike on Wednesday.
Governor Bill Lee announced the change on Saturday, sharing the news in a joint statement with Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada. Strada said that his stepping down is “in the best interests” of the state, and called the ongoing investigation into the incident “entirely appropriate and necessary”. Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer, survived two injections and is now in critical condition at a Tennessee hospital as her lawyers seek to commute her sentence. “Commissioner Strada has served with integrity, and I appreciate his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment,” Lee said.
Lee has ordered an independent review into Pike’s attempted execution and he halted all executions in the state for the year.
Pike is being treated at a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee where doctor are attempting to clear the drugs used during the execution from her body, according to legal filings.
She was injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday but remained alive. She was then sent to hospital in an ambulance. While receiving the two doses, “she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly throughout the procedure”, her lawyers said.
As of Thursday night, she was unconscious, intubated and on a ventilator.
The state’s Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying “the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out”.
Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong. Her lawyers filed an emergency motion on Friday to preserve “any and all evidence” related to her failed execution.
Pike’s attorneys previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins - meant there was a risk she would experience “unnecessary” pain and suffering during a lethal injection.
The attempted execution went ahead after multiple failed, last-minute legal challenges by Pike’s lawyers.
The US Supreme Court rejected two separate efforts to stop the lethal injection.
Tennessee’s governor also denied a clemency request from Pike, the only woman on the state’s death row.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer in 1995.

The head of Tennessee’s prison system is set to resign after the botched execution of Christa Pike, who remains unconscious and on a ventilator at a Nashville-area hospital.
Gov. Bill Lee on Saturday announced Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, will step down from his post later this month. The staffing shakeup comes just three days after Pike survived a double dose of pentobarbital, which the state uses to execute prisoners.
Lee has also called for a full, independent review of what may have gone wrong, and he has pressed pause on the last execution the state had scheduled for this year.
“Commissioner Strada has served with integrity, and I appreciate his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment,” the governor said in a statement.
“I have accepted his decision to step down and am grateful for his commitment to ensuring a smooth leadership transition,” he continued. “I thank Commissioner Strada for his dedicated service to Tennessee and pray God’s blessings over him in the days ahead.”
Pike, now 50 and fighting for her life, was convicted of first-degree murder for brutally torturing and killing Colleen Slemmer, 19, in a wooded area of the University of Tennessee agricultural campus on Jan. 12, 1995.
On the night of the attack, Pike, her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, 17, and an acquaintance, Shadolla Peterson, 18, lured Slemmer to an isolated area behind the agricultural campus steam plant. There, Pike and Shipp violently tortured Slemmer before killing her, while Peterson acted as lookout.
Pike’s legal team on Saturday praised Strada’s forthcoming exit, but said in a statement, “It does nothing to help Christa now.”
“What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person,” they continued. “We hope the governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system.”
In addition to Pike being intubated and put on a ventilator, her arms were swollen, blistered and bruised from the lethal injection drugs, her attorneys said in an emergency motion filed earlier this week.
“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body,” the emergency motion said.
Strada was appointed commissioner of Tennessee’s Department of Correction by Lee in January 2023, after serving as deputy director of Arizona’s Department of Correction. Strada said in a statement that he believes “the Department carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol,” but that “stepping aside is in the best interest” of the state.

A third schoolmate who was 18 at the time and acted as a lookout testified for the prosecution and received probation.

Tennessee prison Commissioner Frank Strada will resign as the state investigates how death row inmate Christa Pike remained alive after receiving two doses of pentobarbital, an execution failure that left her unconscious and on a ventilator and prompted Gov. Bill Lee to halt further executions in 2026.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
Tennessee’s top corrections official is stepping down following the failed execution of Christa Gail Pike, who survived two doses of the state’s lethal-injection drug and was hospitalized unconscious and dependent on a ventilator.
Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday that Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada had offered his resignation and would leave the agency this month. Lee has ordered an independent investigation into the Sept. 30 execution attempt at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville and halted additional executions for the remainder of 2026. Reuters reported that an interim commissioner will be named later.
“Commissioner Strada has served with integrity, and I appreciate his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment,” Lee said.
Strada defended the department’s personnel while acknowledging that leadership should change as investigators examine what occurred.
He said he believes TDOC staff “carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol” and called the independent review “entirely appropriate and necessary.”
Strada added that “stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward.”
Pike’s attorneys welcomed his departure but said the problems exposed during the execution extend beyond one administrator.
The resignation was “justified,” they said, but “it does nothing to help Christa now.”
“What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person,” her legal team said. “We hope the Governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system.”
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate at the Knoxville Job Corps program. Pike was 18 at the time of the crime and received her death sentence in 1996.
Had the Sept. 30 execution been completed, Pike would have become the first woman put to death by Tennessee in at least two centuries.
Instead, a process that had already been delayed for hours by last-minute court proceedings ended with Pike being removed from the prison by ambulance and taken to a Nashville-area hospital.
Her execution originally was scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. A federal appeals court stopped it about an hour beforehand while considering a final legal challenge. Tennessee appealed, and the U.S. Supreme Court later cleared the state to proceed. Roughly 90 minutes after that ruling, the execution chamber was opened to witnesses with Pike strapped to the gurney. The Associated Press reported that she eventually received two doses of pentobarbital but continued breathing.
Before the drug was administered, the execution team allegedly experienced significant difficulty establishing intravenous access.
Pike’s attorneys said at least seven needles were used while personnel attempted to obtain access to her veins. Court filings described Pike herself attempting to assist the execution team.
“At one point, Ms. Pike herself offered guidance on where the IV team could attempt access; one needle was bent in a 90-degree angle when it was removed,” her attorneys wrote.
During the process, Pike complained about the condition of her arm.
“My arm feels like it’s about to burst open,” she said, according to the filing.
At another point, she asked, “Does this happen like that?”
Her attorneys had previously warned state officials that Pike suffered from thrombocytosis, a condition involving elevated platelets, and had unusually difficult venous access. They argued before the execution that those conditions could make lethal injection unusually problematic.
Once the execution began, Pike’s lawyers allege that the IV lines were not correctly positioned or did not remain inside the veins.
Their emergency filing contends that pentobarbital may consequently have entered surrounding tissue rather than flowing properly into her bloodstream.
Pike’s arms were later described by her attorneys as swollen, burned and blistered. By Oct. 1, she was unconscious, intubated and receiving mechanical ventilation while medical personnel worked to remove pentobarbital from her system.
The state has not publicly established the cause of the failure.
The Department of Correction issued a brief statement after the execution attempt defending its actions.
“The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office,” the department said. “The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening.”
TDOC said Pike was transported to an off-site medical facility after the protocol ended.
Pike’s lawyers filed an emergency motion Oct. 2 in Davidson County Chancery Court seeking to preserve evidence connected to the execution attempt.
The request covers physical evidence, records and other material that could help determine what happened inside the death chamber. The attorneys also requested an expedited hearing.
WSMV reported that the filing alleges the state may have prepared the lethal drugs early that morning, even though court proceedings delayed their administration until many hours later. The defense wants records preserved that could establish when the pentobarbital was prepared, how it was handled and precisely how the IV lines were placed.
As of Oct. 3, no ruling had been announced on the request for an expedited hearing.
The episode is the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to complete a scheduled execution.
In May, officials abandoned the execution of Tony Carruthers after medical personnel successfully placed one IV but were unable to establish the required second line despite trying several locations. Lee ordered the state to wait at least one year before attempting Carruthers’ execution again.
The failures have renewed scrutiny of Tennessee’s execution system only a few years after an earlier investigation found repeated problems with the state’s procedures.
In 2022, Lee suspended executions after discovering that the state had failed to properly test lethal-injection drugs as required under its own protocol. An independent investigation led by former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton later found that Tennessee had repeatedly failed to comply with its execution procedures.
The state eventually abandoned its three-drug lethal-injection protocol and adopted a single-drug system using pentobarbital.
Four inmates have been executed in Tennessee since executions resumed in 2025, according to the Department of Correction. Pike’s failed execution has now led Lee to again suspend the process while an outside review is conducted.
The governor has said investigators should take whatever time is required to determine precisely what happened.
“It needs to be done thoroughly and however long that takes, whatever process is required to make sure we get to the very end of it and all the questions are answered,” Lee said.
Pike’s case drew national attention even before the failed execution because of the severity of Slemmer’s murder, Pike’s age at the time of the crime and the rarity of executions involving women.
Prosecutors said Pike and two others lured Slemmer to an isolated area near the University of Tennessee agricultural campus in Knoxville in January 1995. Slemmer was beaten, cut and killed during a prolonged attack.
Pike was convicted of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.
Slemmer’s relatives have waited more than three decades for the sentence to be carried out, and her mother was among those who witnessed the Sept. 30 attempt.
Pike’s attorneys, meanwhile, have renewed calls for Lee to commute her death sentence following what they describe as an unprecedented ordeal.
The failed execution has also intensified questions about what Tennessee’s protocol requires when the maximum authorized quantity of pentobarbital fails to cause death. Once the two available doses had been administered, TDOC said its protocol provided no additional execution procedure.
The immediate focus has now shifted from carrying out Pike’s sentence to preserving evidence, determining the extent of her injuries and establishing why the lethal-injection process failed.
Strada’s resignation represents the first major leadership consequence.
The independent investigation ordered by Lee will now examine an execution in which the state says its personnel followed the approved protocol while the condemned inmate’s attorneys allege that fundamental problems with IV placement caused the lethal drug to enter her tissue rather than her bloodstream.
Until that review is completed, Tennessee’s execution chamber will remain inactive.

sources.news_title: Failed Christa Pike execution prompts resignation of Tennessee prisons chief
sources.text:
The head of Tennessee's prison system has resigned days after the state's failed execution of death row inmate Christa Pike, as officials face mounting questions about how two doses of a lethal injection drug failed to carry out her death sentence.
Republican Governor Bill Lee announced Saturday that Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner (TDOC) Frank Strada will step down later this month. Strada took over the department in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections.
The resignation comes as the state launches an independent review into the September 30 execution attempt, which left Pike hospitalized, unconscious and reliant on a ventilator, according to court filings cited by the Associated Press.
Strada said in a statement to the AP that stepping aside was "in the best interests" of Tennessee while investigators determine what went wrong during the execution.
“I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary, and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred,” he added.
Pike's attorneys told Newsweek in an emailed statement Saturday, "The resignation of Commissioner Strada is justified, but it does nothing to help Christa now."
"What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason from the TN Office of the Post Conviction Defender, and Stephen Ferrell and Luke Ihnen from Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee, Pike's legal team said. "We hope the Governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system."
On Saturday afternoon, Lee's office announced that former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton would lead the review.
Laura Porter, the executive director at the U.S. Campaign to End the Death Penalty, told Newsweek in emailed statement that "attorneys and community leaders across Tennessee have been trying for some time to get the governor and the administration to take seriously the huge problems with the competency of the state’s execution process," adding that they were ignored.
"Hopefully, this is the beginning of accountability and an end to secrecy that enables these debacles,” Porter said.
When reached via email Saturday, the Communications Director for the TDOC referred Newsweek to the governor's office. Newsweek reached out to Lee’s office as well as Strada by email Saturday for further comment.
The failed execution has reignited debate over lethal injection protocols and the future of capital punishment in the United States.
Tennessee has halted its remaining executions for 2026 following the incident, while legal experts and death penalty advocates have questioned whether the state can attempt to execute Pike a second time.
Pike's case is highly unusual because inmates who receive a full execution protocol but survive are exceedingly rare in modern American capital punishment. Legal scholars previously told Newsweek that historical precedent suggests a second execution attempt could be allowed, though the issue would likely trigger extensive court challenges.
The case has also become a national political issue. President Donald Trump has continued advocating for expanding the death penalty even after Pike's failed execution, saying capital punishment should remain available for major drug traffickers, human traffickers and those convicted of killing police officers.
Previous Incidents Linked to Strada
Corinna Lain, author of Secrets of the Killing State: The Untold Story of Lethal Injection and the George E. Allen Chair in Law at the University of Richmond School of Law, pointed out that this is not the first botched execution incident Strada has been attached out to.
"Frank Strada was the person in charge of Arizona’s department of corrections when it botched three executions in 2022. He left the department shortly after and then was hired to lead Tennessee’s department of corrections," she told Newsweek in an email.
In her book, Lain wrote, "I remember the very same governor, Governor Lee, saying in 2022 that lethal injection was a very important task that needed to be performed correctly, and that that he was showing his commitment to doing it right by changing the leadership at the top—and then finding out that the department of corrections had hired the very same guy who was overseeing botched executions in Arizona.”
During the 2022 execution of Clarence Dixon, officials spent roughly 30 minutes attempting to place an IV before ultimately accessing a vein in his groin. Just a month later, medical personnel struggled to find a suitable vein in Frank Atwood’s his right arm, prompting Atwood to suggest using his hand instead, according to Henry Brean, an Arizona Daily Star reporter who was a witness. There was an unsuccessful attempt to insert an IV line in Murray Hooper's right arm, with the AP reporting that the IV in Hooper's leg was inserted into his femoral artery instead.
The incidents led Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs to pause lethal-injection executions and appoint retired federal Judge David Duncan to conduct an independent review of the state's execution procedures, according to Fox 10 Phoenix. Duncan later said he was removed from the role after concluding that lethal injection was not a viable execution method.
Newsweek reached out to Hobbs and the Arizona DOC by email Saturday for comment.
Christa Pike's Failed Execution
Pike, now 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and murder of fellow Job Corps student Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville. She was set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
According to execution attempt witnesses, Pike remained alive after receiving two doses of pentobarbital. During the procedure she reportedly complained of pain in her arm, later lost consciousness and was transported to a hospital rather than being pronounced dead.
Her attorneys later argued that execution personnel may have failed to properly establish intravenous access, resulting in the drug entering tissue rather than her bloodstream.
In a court filing cited by the AP, lawyers alleged that members of the execution team did not recognize that IV lines may have been improperly placed or that veins had "blown" during the process.
Experts previously told Newsweek there were three leading possible explanations for the failure: the drugs may never have properly reached Pike's bloodstream, the pentobarbital may have been ineffective, or Pike may have experienced an uncommon physiological response to the drug.
Corinna Barrett Lain, a University of Richmond law professor and author of Secrets of the Killing State: The Untold Story of Lethal Injection, told Newsweek recently that Pike's case appears to be unprecedented in the modern era of lethal injection executions.
Lain said inmates have previously survived execution attempts when officials were unable to establish IV access, but she was unaware of another case in which executioners successfully administered the drugs and the inmate nonetheless survived, noting, "We've never had someone who has survived their own execution when the drugs are going into them."
She added that earlier execution failures typically occurred because officials could not access a prisoner's veins before the drugs were delivered.
According to Ferrell, his team warned officials that her medical history and blood condition could make IV access difficult for months prior to the execution, which he noted would raise the risk of a prolonged execution attempt.
Pike's legal team said she remained critically ill after the execution attempt, while court filings stated hospital staff were working to remove the pentobarbital from her system.
History of Execution Failures
Questions surrounding Pike's case have drawn renewed attention to Tennessee's troubled history with executions.
April 2022
Lee halted the execution of Oscar Smith at the last minute after officials discovered the state had failed to follow its own lethal injection protocols. An independent investigation later identified significant flaws in Tennessee's execution procedures.
2022-2025
Tennessee suspended executions while officials reviewed and revised the state's lethal injection procedures following the findings of the independent review. According to NewsNation, executions did not resume until 2025.
May 2026
Officials halted the execution of death row inmate Tony Carruthers after spending more than an hour unsuccessfully attempting to establish intravenous access.
September 30, 2026
The state attempted to execute Pike using pentobarbital. Despite two doses being administered, Pike survived and was rushed to a hospital. Witnesses reported that she continued breathing and making sounds after the injections.
October 2026
Following the failed execution, Lee ordered an independent review and accepted the resignation of prison commissioner Strada.
What Happens Next
The state's independent investigation is expected to examine every aspect of Pike's execution attempt, including the placement of IV lines, the administration of pentobarbital and whether protocol was followed.
Meanwhile, Pike's attorneys are seeking preservation of evidence related to the execution and are expected to challenge any effort to schedule a second execution date. Tennessee prison chief to resign after Christa Pike's failed execution
- Published
The head of prisons in the US state of Tennessee is resigning after the failed execution of death row inmate Christa Pike on Wednesday.
Governor Bill Lee announced the change on Saturday, sharing the news in a joint statement with Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada.
Strada said that his stepping down is "in the best interests" of the state, and called the ongoing investigation into the incident "entirely appropriate and necessary".
Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer, survived two injections and is now in critical condition at a Tennessee hospital as her lawyers seek to commute her sentence.
"Commissioner Strada has served with integrity, and I appreciate his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment," Lee said.
Lee has ordered an independent review into Pike's attempted execution and he halted all executions in the state for the year.
Attorneys for Pike called the resignation "justified" but said "it does nothing to help Christa now".
"What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," Pike's legal team wrote in a statement. "We hope the Governor's call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee's entire death penalty system."
Pike is being treated at a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee, where doctors are attempting to clear the drugs used during the execution from her body, according to legal filings.
She was injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday but remained alive. She was then sent to hospital in an ambulance. While receiving the two doses, "she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly throughout the procedure", her lawyers said.
As of Thursday night, she was unconscious, intubated and on a ventilator.
The state's Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".
Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong. Her lawyers filed an emergency motion on Friday to preserve "any and all evidence" related to her failed execution.
Pike's attorneys previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins - meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection.
The attempted execution went ahead after multiple failed, last-minute legal challenges by Pike's lawyers.
The US Supreme Court rejected two separate efforts to stop the lethal injection.
Tennessee's governor also denied a clemency request from Pike, the only woman on the state's death row.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer in 1995.
She was sentenced to death the following year after a media frenzy around the killing in Knoxville, Tennessee.

The head of Tennessee’s prison system is resigning just days after Christa Pike survived two lethal injection attempts. Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday that Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada will step down later this month, with an interim commissioner to be named at a later date.
The announcement came three days after Pike’s failed execution on Wednesday, September 30, at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Pike was given two doses of pentobarbital, the sedative Tennessee uses for lethal injections, and did not die. She was rushed to the hospital, where her attorneys say she remains unconscious and on a ventilator in critical condition.
Strada said in a statement that stepping aside “is in the best interests” of the state while an independent review determines what went wrong. He did not admit fault. “I continue to believe the Department carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol,” he said.
Lee thanked him on the way out. “I thank Commissioner Strada for his dedicated service to Tennessee and pray God’s blessings over him in the days ahead,” the governor said.
Christa Pike’s legal team was not satisfied. “The resignation of Commissioner Strada is justified, but it does nothing to help Christa now,” her attorneys said. Her lawyers believe problems with the IV lines caused the drug to flow into her body tissue instead of her bloodstream, which would explain why it never took full effect.
The failure was not the first under Strada’s leadership. Pike’s was the second botched execution in Tennessee on his watch this year. Lee appointed Strada in January 2023, and by December 2024 his department had issued the new lethal injection protocols that allowed Tennessee to resume executions. Before coming to Tennessee, Strada served as deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections, where multiple executions under his watch also ran into complications. He previously worked as director of operations for GEO Group, a private prison company.
A former U.S. attorney will lead the independent review of Pike’s attempted execution. Lee has also paused all executions in Tennessee through the end of the year and ordered that Pike’s execution be delayed until at least next year.
Christa Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of 19 year old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow student at a Knoxville job training program for troubled teens. Pike was 18 at the time. She had exhausted all of her appeals, and her execution would have made her the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
Before the execution, Pike’s lawyers had warned the state that a blood disorder made lethal injection especially dangerous for her and asked that she be executed by hanging instead. Since she survived, her legal team has pushed for Tennessee to spare her life entirely.

sources.news_title: Tennessee Prisons Chief Resigns After Christa Pike Execution
sources.text:
NASHVILLE, United States — Frank Strada, the head of the Tennessee prison system, has resigned days after the state failed to execute Christa Gail Pike despite administering two doses of pentobarbital.
Governor Bill Lee announced on Saturday, October 3, 2026, that he had accepted Strada’s resignation as commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Correction.
Strada will leave the post later this month, and the governor will name an interim commissioner.
The departure is the first major leadership change since Wednesday’s execution attempt at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution left Pike alive and requiring emergency medical treatment.
“Commissioner Strada has served with integrity, and I appreciate his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment,” Lee said.
Strada said he believed department personnel had followed the state’s prescribed execution procedure but concluded that leaving his position was appropriate while an outside investigation was conducted.
“Stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward,” he said.
Independent Review Ordered
Lee has appointed former United States Attorney Ed Stanton to examine what went wrong during Pike’s execution attempt.
Stanton previously conducted a review of Tennessee’s execution system after Lee suspended an execution in 2022.
That investigation found failures by the state to follow its own lethal-injection procedures.
Lee has now halted executions in Tennessee for the remainder of 2026 while the latest review proceeds.
The Department of Correction maintained immediately after Wednesday’s attempt that it had followed every step of the state’s approved protocol.
It said the procedure did not permit officials to take additional execution measures after those already carried out.
Pike was then transported from the prison to an outside hospital.
Her lawyers said in a court filing on Friday that she was unconscious, intubated, and being kept alive with a mechanical ventilator.
They said doctors were working to remove pentobarbital from her system.
No more recent public medical update had been issued by Saturday.
Two Doses Failed to Complete Execution
Pike, 50, had been scheduled to die for the 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old fellow student at a Job Corps programme.
The execution initially faced a last-minute delay when a federal appeals court issued a stay. The United States Supreme Court later lifted that order, permitting Tennessee to proceed.
Officials administered two rounds of pentobarbital, the drug used under Tennessee’s single-drug lethal-injection protocol, but Pike remained alive.
Her lawyers contend that the intravenous lines did not properly deliver the drug into her bloodstream and say prison authorities had been warned beforehand that her small veins and a blood disorder, thrombocytosis, could make intravenous access difficult.
The state has not accepted that explanation, and the independent review has yet to determine why the execution failed.
The episode would have marked Tennessee’s first execution of a woman in more than two centuries.
Second Failed Execution This Year
Wednesday’s events followed another unsuccessful execution attempt under Strada’s leadership.
In May, Tennessee halted the execution of Tony Carruthers after staff succeeded in placing one intravenous line but were unable to establish the secondary line required by the state’s protocol.
That execution was postponed for at least a year.
Tennessee had revised its lethal-injection procedures under Strada, adopting pentobarbital as its sole execution drug in late 2024.
At the time, Strada said he was confident the new procedure could be carried out in accordance with departmental policy and state law.
Four prisoners have been executed in Tennessee since executions resumed under the revised system.
Strada Took Charge in 2023
Lee appointed Strada to lead the Department of Correction in January 2023 following a previous review of Tennessee’s execution practices.
Before moving to Tennessee, Strada had been deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections, overseeing prison operations and other programmes.
He had also spent nearly three decades with the Federal Bureau of Prisons.
His Arizona tenure included oversight responsibilities during the state’s return to executions in 2022.
Several of those executions involved difficulties establishing intravenous access, according to court records and witness accounts cited by The Associated Press.
Pike’s lawyers said Strada’s resignation did not resolve the broader questions raised by what happened inside the Tennessee execution chamber.
“What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person,” her legal team said.
The lawyers said they hoped Lee’s independent investigation would examine the state’s wider death-penalty procedures.
Stanton’s review is now expected to determine whether Tennessee followed its protocol, why two administrations of pentobarbital failed to kill Pike, and what changes may be required before executions can resume.
